claim: Sleep has been conserved throughout evolution.
source: Sleep has been conserved throughout evolution; however, the molecular and neuronal mechanisms of sleep are largely unknown.
evidence: This is a general statement about sleep conservation presented in the abstract without specific experimental data from this study.

claim: The molecular and neuronal mechanisms of sleep are largely unknown.
source: Sleep has been conserved throughout evolution; however, the molecular and neuronal mechanisms of sleep are largely unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The hypothalamic hypocretin/orexin (Hcrt) neurons regulate sleep/wake states, feeding, stress, and reward.
source: The hypothalamic hypocretin/orexin (Hcrt) neurons regulate sleep\wake states, feeding, stress, and reward.
evidence: This statement is presented as established knowledge about Hcrt neurons.

claim: Dozens of Hcrt-neuron–specific transcripts were identified using fluorescence cell sorting and RNA-seq in hcrt:EGFP zebrafish.
source: To elucidate the mechanism that enables these various functions and to identify sleep regulators, we combined fluorescence cell sorting and RNA-seq in hcrt:EGFP zebrafish. Dozens of Hcrt-neuron–specific transcripts were identified and comprehensive high-resolution imaging revealed gene-specific localization in all or subsets of Hcrt neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental approach described in the manuscript using FACS and RNA-seq.

claim: Comprehensive high-resolution imaging revealed gene-specific localization in all or subsets of Hcrt neurons.
source: Dozens of Hcrt-neuron–specific transcripts were identified and comprehensive high-resolution imaging revealed gene-specific localization in all or subsets of Hcrt neurons.
evidence: This is supported by the ISH and immunofluorescence data shown in the figures.

claim: Clusters of Hcrt-neuron–specific genes are predicted to be regulated by shared transcription factors.
source: Clusters of Hcrt-neuron–specific genes are predicted to be regulated by shared transcription factors.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis of transcription factor binding sites.

claim: Hcrt neurons are heterogeneous.
source: These findings show that Hcrt neurons are heterogeneous and that integrative molecular mechanisms orchestrate their diverse functions.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observation that different genes are expressed in subsets of Hcrt neurons.

claim: Integrative molecular mechanisms orchestrate the diverse functions of Hcrt neurons.
source: These findings show that Hcrt neurons are heterogeneous and that integrative molecular mechanisms orchestrate their diverse functions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings regarding gene expression patterns and transcription factors.

claim: The voltage-gated potassium channel Kcnh4a is expressed in all Hcrt neurons.
source: The voltage-gated potassium channel Kcnh4a, which is expressed in all Hcrt neurons, was silenced by the CRISPR-mediated gene inactivation system.
evidence: This is supported by ISH and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3D-D'',K-K''.

claim: Kcnh4a was silenced by the CRISPR-mediated gene inactivation system.
source: The voltage-gated potassium channel Kcnh4a, which is expressed in all Hcrt neurons, was silenced by the CRISPR-mediated gene inactivation system.
evidence: This is supported by the methods and results showing generation of kcnh4a mutants.

claim: The mutant kcnh4a (kcnh4a-/-) larvae showed reduced sleep time and consolidation, specifically during the night.
source: The mutant kcnh4a (kcnh4a-/-) larvae showed reduced sleep time and consolidation, specifically during the night, suggesting that Kcnh4a regulates sleep.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Kcnh4a regulates sleep.
source: The mutant kcnh4a (kcnh4a-/-) larvae showed reduced sleep time and consolidation, specifically during the night, suggesting that Kcnh4a regulates sleep.
evidence: This is inferred from the sleep phenotype observed in kcnh4a mutants.

claim: Sleep disorders affect a large portion of the world's population.
source: Sleep is a fundamental behavior that benefits the brain and sleep disorders affect a large portion of the world's population (Shepard et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The hypothalamus centralizes sleep regulation and maintains essential physiological processes, including growth, reproduction, body temperature, stress, reward, feeding, and circadian rhythms.
source: The hypothalamus centralizes sleep regulation and maintains essential physiological processes, including growth, reproduction, body temperature, stress, reward, feeding, and circadian rhythms (Salin-Pascual et al., 2001; Mignot et al., 2002; Saper et al., 2005; Saper, 2006; Begg and Woods, 2013; Dietrich and Horvath, 2013; Sternson, 2013; Muindi et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: The suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) is the master circadian oscillator.
source: Some of these nuclei, such as the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), which is the master circadian oscillator (Welsh et al., 2010), have been well characterized both anatomically and physiologically, while the neuronal identity and function of other nuclei is less understood (Rolls et al., 2010; Sakurai and Mieda, 2011; Dietrich and Horvath, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Welsh et al., 2010.

claim: The hypocretin neurons secrete the Hcrt neuropeptides and are located in the lateral hypothalamus (LH).
source: The hypocretin (Hcrt, also called orexin) neurons secrete the Hcrt neuropeptides and are located in the lateral hypothalamus (LH).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Hcrt neurons.

claim: Hcrt neurons project to wide areas in the brain, including the tuberomammillary nucleus, paraventricular thalamic nucleus, arcuate nucleus, and monoaminergic nuclei.
source: These hypothalamic neurons project to wide areas in the brain, including the tuberomammillary nucleus, paraventricular thalamic nucleus, arcuate nucleus, and monoaminergic nuclei (Sakurai, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Sakurai, 2007.

claim: Hcrt neurons were initially implicated in feeding behavior and sleep/wake cycles.
source: They were initially implicated in feeding behavior and sleep\wake cycles (de Lecea et al., 1998; Sakurai et al., 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to de Lecea et al., 1998 and Sakurai et al., 1998.

claim: Loss of Hcrt neurons causes the sleep disorder narcolepsy.
source: Their role in sleep regulation was further strengthened since loss of Hcrt neurons causes the sleep disorder narcolepsy, which is characterized by sleep\wake fragmentation, increased body mass, and cataplexy (loss of muscle tone, often triggered by emotional stimuli) (Chemelli et al., 1999; Lin et al., 1999; Peyron et al., 2000; Schuld et al., 2000; Adamantidis et al., 2007; Burgess et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Narcolepsy is characterized by sleep/wake fragmentation, increased body mass, and cataplexy.
source: Their role in sleep regulation was further strengthened since loss of Hcrt neurons causes the sleep disorder narcolepsy, which is characterized by sleep\wake fragmentation, increased body mass, and cataplexy (loss of muscle tone, often triggered by emotional stimuli) (Chemelli et al., 1999; Lin et al., 1999; Peyron et al., 2000; Schuld et al., 2000; Adamantidis et al., 2007; Burgess et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: The function of Hcrt neurons includes regulation of energy homeostasis, pain, emotion, stress response, and reward.
source: However, extensive research showed that the function of Hcrt neurons is much broader and also includes regulation of energy homeostasis, pain, emotion, stress response, and reward (Sakurai, 2007; Rolls et al., 2010; Boutrel et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A single hcrt gene encodes for the precursor polypeptide prepro-Hcrt, which is cleaved to produce two Hcrt neuropeptides.
source: A single hcrt gene encodes for the precursor polypeptide prepro-Hcrt, which is cleaved to produce two Hcrt neuropeptides.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Hcrt gene and peptides.

claim: The actions of the Hcrt neuropeptides are mediated via two Hcrt G-protein–coupled receptors (Hcrtrs).
source: The actions of the Hcrt neuropeptides are mediated via two Hcrt G-protein–coupled receptors (Hcrtrs) (Sakurai, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Sakurai, 2007.

claim: The synaptic release of glutamate from Hcrt neurons affects the activity of post-synaptic target neurons.
source: In addition, the synaptic release of glutamate from Hcrt neurons has been shown to affect the activity of post-synaptic target neurons (Henny et al., 2010; Schone et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Henny et al., 2010 and Schone et al., 2012.

claim: Three studies have described the gene-expression profile of Hcrt neurons in rodents.
source: Three studies have described the gene-expression profile of Hcrt neurons in rodents (Honda et al., 2009; Cvetkovic-Lopes et al., 2010; Dalal et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to three previous studies.

claim: The zebrafish has become a valuable model for the study of specific neuronal populations in live animals.
source: The zebrafish has become a valuable model for the study of specific neuronal populations in live animals. It is a simple and diurnal vertebrate that combines powerful genetic tools with conserved anatomy and function of the brain (Severi et al., 2014; Thiele et al., 2014; Romano et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Behavioral criteria have been used to characterize sleep in zebrafish.
source: In the last two decades, behavioral criteria have been used to characterize sleep in zebrafish (Zhdanova et al., 2001; Prober et al., 2006; Yokogawa et al., 2007; Sigurgeirsson et al., 2011; Elbaz et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: The zebrafish Hcrt neurons are located in the hypothalamus.
source: Similar to mammals, the Hcrt neurons are located in the zebrafish hypothalamus but, in contrast to mammals, the zebrafish Hcrt system contains only a few neurons, making it a relatively simple system to study (Kaslin et al., 2004; Faraco et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Kaslin et al., 2004 and Faraco et al., 2006.

claim: The zebrafish Hcrt system contains only a few neurons.
source: Similar to mammals, the Hcrt neurons are located in the zebrafish hypothalamus but, in contrast to mammals, the zebrafish Hcrt system contains only a few neurons, making it a relatively simple system to study (Kaslin et al., 2004; Faraco et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Kaslin et al., 2004 and Faraco et al., 2006.

claim: The Hcrt system regulates sleep and wake in zebrafish.
source: Functional studies using Hcrt-neuron–specific genetic ablation, as well as genetic manipulation of the hcrt ligand and receptors, showed that the Hcrt system regulates sleep and wake in zebrafish (Prober et al., 2006; Yokogawa et al., 2007; Elbaz et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The zebrafish Hcrt neurons induce feeding behavior.
source: In addition, the zebrafish Hcrt neurons induce feeding behavior (Yokobori et al., 2011), as is the case in mammals.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Yokobori et al., 2011.

claim: The LIM homeobox transcription factor Lhx9 is widely expressed in the brain, including in the Hcrt neurons.
source: Similar to mammals (Dalal et al., 2013), microarray gene-expression analysis revealed that the LIM homeobox transcription factor Lhx9, which is widely expressed in the brain, including in the Hcrt neurons, can induce the specification of Hcrt neurons (Liu et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Dalal et al., 2013 and Liu et al., 2015.

claim: Lhx9 can induce the specification of Hcrt neurons.
source: Similar to mammals (Dalal et al., 2013), microarray gene-expression analysis revealed that the LIM homeobox transcription factor Lhx9, which is widely expressed in the brain, including in the Hcrt neurons, can induce the specification of Hcrt neurons (Liu et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2015.

claim: The hcrt:EGFP zebrafish enables specific visualization and manipulation of the entire population of Hcrt neurons (16-20 cells per larva).
source: In order to isolate the Hcrt neurons, the transgenic hcrt:EGFP zebrafish (Appelbaum et al., 2009), which enables specific visualization and manipulation of the entire population of Hcrt neurons (16-–20 cells per larva), was used.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Appelbaum et al., 2009 and describes the transgenic line used.

claim: EGFP-positive (EGFP+) cells from hcrt:EGFP larvae were sorted by FACS.
source: At 7 dpf, the heads of hcrt:EGFP larvae (Figure 1A,B) were dissociated, and EGFP-positive (EGFP+) cells from the cell suspension sample (Figure 1C) were sorted by FACS (Figure 1D–G).
evidence: This is supported by the methods described and Figure 1.

claim: hcrt and egfp were detected in EGFP+ cells but not in EGFP- cells.
source: While hcrt and egfp were detected in EGFP+ cells, they were not amplified in EGFP- cells (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The EGFP+ cells mostly contain Hcrt neurons.
source: These results show that the EGFP+ cells mostly contain Hcrt neurons, while the EGFP- group contains a heterogeneous population of cells from the whole larva head.
evidence: This is inferred from the RT-PCR validation showing hcrt expression in EGFP+ cells.

claim: The EGFP- group contains a heterogeneous population of cells from the whole larva head.
source: These results show that the EGFP+ cells mostly contain Hcrt neurons, while the EGFP- group contains a heterogeneous population of cells from the whole larva head.
evidence: This is inferred from the FACS procedure and the absence of hcrt expression in EGFP- cells.

claim: The bioinformatic analysis identified 20 transcripts that were preferentially expressed in Hcrt cells (p<0.01).
source: These criteria stipulated a high level of specificity to the EGFP+ samples relative to the control samples. The bioinformatic analysis identified 20 transcripts that were found to meet these criteria (p<0.01, Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the RNA-seq data and bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Among the 20 transcripts identified, 12 were annotated genes and 8 were non-annotated transcripts.
source: Among the 20 transcripts, 12 were annotated genes and 8 were non-annotated transcripts.
evidence: This is based on the bioinformatic analysis of the RNA-seq data.

claim: The hcrt gene was expressed at a level of 300 TPM in EGFP+ and below 10 TPM in both control samples.
source: Notably, the hcrt gene was expressed at a level of 300 TPM in EGFP+ and below 10 TPM in both control samples.
evidence: This is based on the RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: The identification of the hcrt gene confirmed the specificity of the cell sorting, the RNA-seq, and the bioinformatic analysis.
source: The identification of an hcrt gene confirmed the specificity of the cell sorting, the RNA-seq, and the bioinformatic analysis.
evidence: This is inferred from the expected high expression of hcrt in EGFP+ cells.

claim: Nine candidate genes were found to be expressed in the hypothalamic area.
source: Nine of them were found to be expressed in the hypothalamic area (hcrt, star, dennd1b, kcnh4a, fam46a, si:dkey-58b18.8, cuff23873.1, npvf, and npffr; Figure 2B–M).
evidence: This is supported by ISH data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Five transcripts (adra, ptgs2b, grpr, cuff64723, and cuff77494) could not be amplified.
source: Five transcripts (adra, ptgs2b, grpr, cuff64723, and cuff77494,) could not be amplified, and the expression of six transcripts (elovl7b, cuff34876, cuff70256, cuff442204, cuff57637, and cuff77484) was not detected at the 2 dpf larval stage.
evidence: This is based on the ISH experiments performed.

claim: The expression of six transcripts (elovl7b, cuff34876, cuff70256, cuff442204, cuff57637, and cuff77484) was not detected at the 2 dpf larval stage.
source: Five transcripts (adra, ptgs2b, grpr, cuff64723, and cuff77494,) could not be amplified, and the expression of six transcripts (elovl7b, cuff34876, cuff70256, cuff442204, cuff57637, and cuff77484) was not detected at the 2 dpf larval stage.
evidence: This is based on the ISH experiments performed.

claim: Only elovl7b showed a detectable expression in the hypothalamus in adults.
source: To test whether these genes were expressed in later developmental stages, their expression was studied in adults. However, only elovl7b showed a detectable expression in the hypothalamus (Figure 3J–J").
evidence: This is supported by ISH data in adult brain sections shown in Figure 3J-J".

claim: The hypothalamic expression pattern of the candidate genes was similar to the expression pattern of hcrt.
source: The hypothalamic expression pattern of the candidate genes was similar to the expression pattern of hcrt (Figure 2B), suggesting that the candidate genes may be expressed in Hcrt neurons.
evidence: This is based on comparison of ISH patterns shown in Figure 2.

claim: Relaxed bioinformatic parameters revealed 212 transcripts that met the criteria (p<0.01).
source: Thus, in order to find more Hcrt-neuron–specific genes, we relaxed the bioinformatic parameters to 10 TPM and 3.6 times higher abundance in EGFP+ cells than in the control groups. This analysis revealed 212 transcripts that met the criteria (p<0.01, Figure 2—source data 1), among them, 146 were non-annotated (called cuff-serial number) and 66 were annotated genes.
evidence: This is based on the bioinformatic analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: Among the 212 transcripts, 146 were non-annotated and 66 were annotated genes.
source: This analysis revealed 212 transcripts that met the criteria (p<0.01, Figure 2—source data 1), among them, 146 were non-annotated (called cuff-serial number) and 66 were annotated genes.
evidence: This is based on the bioinformatic analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: Some of the non-annotated transcripts were likely long, non-coding RNA (lncRNA).
source: Some of the non-annotated transcripts were likely long, non-coding RNA (lncRNA) since they were longer than 200 bp, did not include a coding sequence, and were located in intergenic regions (Perkel, 2013).
evidence: This is inferred from the characteristics of the transcripts and supported by a citation.

claim: lncRNAs regulate transcription and epigenetic processes and may be involved in the regulation of splicing and translation.
source: lncRNAs regulate transcription and epigenetic processes and may be involved in the regulation of splicing and translation (Mercer et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Mercer et al., 2009.

claim: Eight transcripts (star, dennd1b, kcnh4a, fam46a, hmx3, zgc171844, lhx9, and si:dkey-58b18.8) co-localized with EGFP in Hcrt neurons.
source: Double staining showed that among the 11 transcripts tested, 8 transcripts (star, dennd1b, kcnh4a, fam46a, hmx3, zgc171844, lhx9, and si:dkey-58b18.8) co-localized with EGFP in Hcrt neurons (Figure 3B–I'').
evidence: This is supported by double ISH and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3.

claim: kcnh4a, hmx3, lhx9 and dennd1b were expressed in most Hcrt neurons.
source: While kcnh4a, hmx3, lhx9 and dennd1b were expressed in most Hcrt neurons, star, fam46a, and zgc171844, were expressed in a subset of the Hcrt neurons.
evidence: This is based on the co-localization analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: star, fam46a, and zgc171844 were expressed in a subset of the Hcrt neurons.
source: While kcnh4a, hmx3, lhx9 and dennd1b were expressed in most Hcrt neurons, star, fam46a, and zgc171844, were expressed in a subset of the Hcrt neurons.
evidence: This is based on the co-localization analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: si:dkey-58b18.8 demonstrated relatively weak expression that was predominantly apparent in Hcrt neurons.
source: In contrast, si:dkey-58b18.8 demonstrated relatively weak expression that was predominantly apparent in Hcrt neurons (Figure 3E–E'').
evidence: This is based on the ISH and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3E-E".

claim: kcnh4a and elovl7b are detected in all Hcrt neurons in adults.
source: Double staining in adults showed that kcnh4a and elovl7b are detected in all Hcrt neurons, while dennd1b is expressed in about half of the Hcrt neurons and zgc171844 in about a third of the neurons.
evidence: This is based on double staining in adult brain sections shown in Figure 3J-M".

claim: dennd1b is expressed in about half of the Hcrt neurons in adults.
source: Double staining in adults showed that kcnh4a and elovl7b are detected in all Hcrt neurons, while dennd1b is expressed in about half of the Hcrt neurons and zgc171844 in about a third of the neurons.
evidence: This is based on double staining in adult brain sections shown in Figure 3J-M".

claim: zgc171844 is expressed in about a third of the Hcrt neurons in adults.
source: Double staining in adults showed that kcnh4a and elovl7b are detected in all Hcrt neurons, while dennd1b is expressed in about half of the Hcrt neurons and zgc171844 in about a third of the neurons.
evidence: This is based on double staining in adult brain sections shown in Figure 3J-M".

claim: The spatial expression of transcripts in subpopulations of Hcrt neurons indicates that Hcrt neurons are not a uniform population but rather heterogeneous neurons.
source: The spatial expression of these transcripts in subpopulations of Hcrt neurons indicates that Hcrt neurons are not a uniform population but rather heterogeneous neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that different genes are expressed in different subsets of Hcrt neurons.

claim: Three candidate transcripts (cuff.23873, npvf, and npffr) labeled distinct hypothalamic populations of neurons that intermingled with Hcrt neurons, but co-localization was not detected.
source: However, three candidate transcripts (cuff.23873, npvf, and npffr; Figure 2H–J) labeled distinct hypothalamic populations of neurons that intermingled with Hcrt neurons, but co-localization was not detected (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by ISH and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4.

claim: These cell populations were located in the immediate vicinity of the Hcrt neurons in the hypothalamus.
source: These cell populations were located in the immediate vicinity of the Hcrt neurons in the hypothalamus.
evidence: This is based on the anatomical observations shown in Figure 4.

claim: npvf showed a specific hypothalamic expression pattern.
source: While, cufff.23873 (Figure 4A–C'') and npffr (Figure 4D–F'') were also expressed in the forebrain area, npvf (Figure 4G–I'') showed a specific hypothalamic expression pattern.
evidence: This is supported by ISH data shown in Figure 4G-I".

claim: A map of possible TF binding sites was generated based on the 48 most enriched transcripts.
source: To identify candidate TFs that can regulate multiple Hcrt-neuron–specific genes, a map of possible TF binding sites was generated based on the 48 most enriched transcripts.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis of regulatory sequences.

claim: This analysis revealed 68 putative TFs.
source: This analysis revealed 68 putative TFs (Figure 5A and Figure 5—source data 1), among them, 13 showed significant enrichment in the top 48 Hcrt-specific transcripts (p<0.005, Figure 5A) including nr6a1, which is a regulator of hcrt in mice (Tanaka et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: 13 TFs showed significant enrichment in the top 48 Hcrt-specific transcripts (p<0.005).
source: This analysis revealed 68 putative TFs (Figure 5A and Figure 5—source data 1), among them, 13 showed significant enrichment in the top 48 Hcrt-specific transcripts (p<0.005, Figure 5A) including nr6a1, which is a regulator of hcrt in mice (Tanaka et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: nr6a1 is a regulator of hcrt in mice.
source: This analysis revealed 68 putative TFs (Figure 5A and Figure 5—source data 1), among them, 13 showed significant enrichment in the top 48 Hcrt-specific transcripts (p<0.005, Figure 5A) including nr6a1, which is a regulator of hcrt in mice (Tanaka et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Tanaka et al., 2010.

claim: The heat shock transcription factor 1 (hsf1) is predicted to regulate 25 Hcrt-neuron–enriched genes.
source: For example, the heat shock transcription factor 1 (hsf1) is predicted to regulate 25 Hcrt-neuron–enriched genes: hcrt, ptgs2, ttn, hspa1l, grpr, elovl7b, slc4a1, lhx9, c16orf45, soat2, tsen54, nos1, rfx4, syt10, trpc7, ntng1, cacng4, myh4, dennd1b, sgsm1, pde2a, wscd1, adra1a, kcnh4a, and hmx3.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic prediction of TF binding sites.

claim: hsf1 is expressed in Hcrt neurons.
source: To test whether this predicted TF is expressed in Hcrt neurons, fluorescent ISH, using a probe for hsf1, and fluorescent immunostaining using an antibody against EGFP, were performed on the brain section of adult hcrt:EGFP zebrafish (Figure 5B–C''). This assay showed wide brain expression of hsf1 and confirmed that hsf1 is also expressed in Hcrt neurons.
evidence: This is supported by ISH and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5B-C".

claim: hsf1 is a key activator of stress conditions in mammals.
source: In mammals, hsf1 is a key activator of stress conditions, and the Hsf1 null mice showed major brain morphological alterations (Santos and Saraiva, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Santos and Saraiva, 2004.

claim: hsf1 is essential for recovery from ischemic injury in the zebrafish brain.
source: In zebrafish, hsf1 is essential for recovery from ischemic injury in the brain (Tucker et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Tucker et al., 2011.

claim: ap-2 is required for sleep-like behavior in C. elegans.
source: In addition, ap-2, a TF that is required for sleep-like behavior in C. elegans (Turek et al., 2013), was predicted to regulate the transcription of 13 Hcrt neuron-specific genes (Figure 5A).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Turek et al., 2013.

claim: ap-2 was predicted to regulate the transcription of 13 Hcrt neuron-specific genes.
source: In addition, ap-2, a TF that is required for sleep-like behavior in C. elegans (Turek et al., 2013), was predicted to regulate the transcription of 13 Hcrt neuron-specific genes (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic prediction shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Two kcnh4 genes are present in zebrafish: kcnh4a located in chromosome 3 and kcnh4b located in chromosome 12.
source: Two kcnh4 are present in zebrafish: kcnh4a (KR733682) located in chromosome 3 and kcnh4b (XM_690738) located in chromosome 12.
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis.

claim: kcnh4a is expressed specifically in the forebrain and hypothalamus in larvae.
source: In contrast to the broad expression of kcnh4b (data not shown), kcnh4a is expressed specifically in the forebrain and hypothalamus in larvae (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by ISH data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: kcnh4a is localized in all Hcrt neurons in both larvae and adults.
source: Double ISH and immunofluorescence staining revealed that kcnh4a is localized in all Hcrt neurons in both larvae and adults (Figure 3D–D'',K–K'') and like Hcrt neurons, hypothalamic kcnh4a-expressing neurons are glutamatergic (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by double staining data shown in Figure 3D-D",K-K" and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Hypothalamic kcnh4a-expressing neurons are glutamatergic.
source: Double ISH and immunofluorescence staining revealed that kcnh4a is localized in all Hcrt neurons in both larvae and adults (Figure 3D–D'',K–K'') and like Hcrt neurons, hypothalamic kcnh4a-expressing neurons are glutamatergic (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by double ISH data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: kcnh4a is localized only a few kilobase pairs (kbp) downstream to hcrt on the genome.
source: Intriguingly, kcnh4a is localized only a few kilobase pairs (kbp) downstream to hcrt on the genome, and a synteny analysis showed that the genomic organization of this locus is conserved with mammals (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by synteny analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The genomic organization of the hcrt-kcnh4a locus is conserved with mammals.
source: Intriguingly, kcnh4a is localized only a few kilobase pairs (kbp) downstream to hcrt on the genome, and a synteny analysis showed that the genomic organization of this locus is conserved with mammals (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by synteny analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In humans, kcnh4a is located only 3782 bp downstream to the hcrt gene.
source: In humans, kcnh4a is located only 3782 bp downstream to the hcrt gene, while in zebrafish, the distance between the genes is 5517 bp (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In zebrafish, the distance between hcrt and kcnh4a is 5517 bp.
source: In humans, kcnh4a is located only 3782 bp downstream to the hcrt gene, while in zebrafish, the distance between the genes is 5517 bp (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: A significant portion of the TFs predicted to regulate hcrt can also bind to kcnh4a regulatory sequences (48 out of 52).
source: Indeed, a significant portion of the TFs predicted to regulate hcrt can also bind to kcnh4a regulatory sequences (48 out of 52, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis of TF binding sites.

claim: The kcnh4a gene consists of 16 exons, which include the 3456 bp coding sequence (CDS).
source: Vector cloning and sequencing of kcnh4a showed that the gene consists of 16 exons, which include the 3456 bp coding sequence (CDS, Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on cloning and sequencing data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The Kcnh4a contains the evolutionarily conserved six S domains that characterize the potassium voltage-gated ion channels.
source: Structural bioinformatic analysis of the protein sequence revealed that the Kcnh4a contains the evolutionarily conserved six S domains that characterize the potassium voltage-gated ion channels (Figure 6B) (Choe, 2002).
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis and supported by a citation to Choe, 2002.

claim: Domains S1–S4 constitute the voltage-gated domain that senses changes in membrane potential.
source: Domains S1–S4 constitute the voltage-gated domain that senses changes in membrane potential (Bezanilla, 2000; Swartz, 2008), whereas domains S5–S6 form the selectivity pore through which ions can flux (Bezanilla, 2000; Choe, 2002; Swartz, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Bezanilla, 2000 and Swartz, 2008.

claim: Domains S5–S6 form the selectivity pore through which ions can flux.
source: Domains S1–S4 constitute the voltage-gated domain that senses changes in membrane potential (Bezanilla, 2000; Swartz, 2008), whereas domains S5–S6 form the selectivity pore through which ions can flux (Bezanilla, 2000; Choe, 2002; Swartz, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Bezanilla, 2000; Choe, 2002; and Swartz, 2008.

claim: The zebrafish Kcnh4a protein is evolutionarily conserved with vertebrate orthologs.
source: Next, phylogenetic analysis revealed that the zebrafish Kcnh4a protein is evolutionarily conserved with vertebrate orthologs (Dereeper et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis and supported by a citation to Dereeper et al., 2008.

claim: A 14 bp deletion mutation was generated in exon 5 of kcnh4a, which encoded part of the pore domain.
source: A 14 bp deletion mutation was generated in exon 5, which encoded part of the pore domain. This deletion introduced a premature stop codon and is predicted to result in truncated protein (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is based on CRISPR mutagenesis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The 14 bp deletion introduced a premature stop codon and is predicted to result in truncated protein.
source: This deletion introduced a premature stop codon and is predicted to result in truncated protein (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is inferred from the sequence analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: qRT-PCR showed a reduction of 59% of kcnh4a mRNA levels in kcnh4a-/- compared to WT-sibling (kcnh4a+/+) 6dpf larvae (p<0.001).
source: Furthermore, quantitative reverse transcription PCR (qRT-PCR) showed a reduction of 59% of kcnh4a mRNA levels in kcnh4a -/- compared to WT-sibling (kcnh4a+/+) 6dpf larvae (p<0.001, Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Larvae from all three genotypes (kcnh4a-/-, kcnh4a+/-, kcnh4a+/+) exhibited rhythmic locomotor activity that peaked during the day.
source: As expected, larvae from all three genotypes exhibited rhythmic locomotor activity that peaked during the day (F[2,180] = 14.98; p<0.0001, mixed-effect model with repeated measures; Figure 7A-A').
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7A-A'.

claim: kcnh4a-/- larvae were slightly hyperactive compared to kcnh4a+/- and kcnh4a+/+ sibling larvae during the day.
source: Notably, kcnh4a-/- larvae were slightly hyperactive (average: 13.84 ± 0.11) compared to kcnh4a+/- (average: 13.29 ± 0.07, t = -4.19, df = 180, p<0.01) and kcnh4a+/+ sibling larvae during the day (average: 12.98 ± 0.1, t = 5.73, df = 180, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 7A-A'.

claim: During the night, the kcnh4a-/- larvae were slightly more active than the kcnh4a+/+ larvae.
source: During the night, the differences in locomotor activity were even lower, and the kcnh4a-/- larvae were slightly more active (average: 8.05 ± 0.13) than the kcnh4a+/+ larvae (average: 7.64 ± 0.12, t = 2.28, df = 180, p<0.05; Figure 7A-A').
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 7A-A'.

claim: The loss of Kcnh4a mildly increases larval locomotor activity, particularly during the day.
source: These results show that the loss of Kcnh4a mildly increases larval locomotor activity, particularly during the day.
evidence: This is inferred from the behavioral data comparing genotypes.

claim: Sleep in larvae was defined as a period of one or more minutes of immobility, which is associated with an increase in arousal threshold.
source: Using well-established behavioral criteria, sleep in larvae was defined as a period of one or more minutes of immobility, which is associated with an increase in arousal threshold (Prober et al., 2006; Elbaz et al., 2012).
evidence: This definition is based on established criteria supported by citations.

claim: Six hours of sleep deprivation (SD) during the night reduced locomotor activity in the following day.
source: A previous study has shown that six hours of sleep deprivation (SD) during the night reduced locomotor activity in the following day (Zhdanova et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Zhdanova et al., 2001.

claim: Six hours of SD during the night increased sleep time during the following day in 6 dpf larvae.
source: Similarly, six hours of SD during the night increased sleep time during the following day in 6 dpf larvae (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Sleep in zebrafish larvae is regulated by circadian and homeostatic processes.
source: Thus, similar to mammals, sleep in zebrafish larvae is regulated by circadian and homeostatic processes.
evidence: This is inferred from the sleep deprivation and recovery experiments.

claim: All three genotypes (kcnh4a-/-,kcnh4a+/-, and kcnh4a+/+) slept more during the night than during the day.
source: Similar to humans, zebrafish are diurnal animals; thus, all three genotypes (kcnh4a-/-,kcnh4a+/-, and kcnh4a+/+) slept more during the night than during the day (F[2,180] = 14.52; p<0.0001, mixed-effect model with repeated measures, Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The amount of sleep was similar in all genotypes during the day.
source: Remarkably, while the amount of sleep was similar in all genotypes during the day (average: kcnh4a-/- = 2.76 ± 0.22; kcnh4a+/- = 2.80 ± 0.14; and kcnh4a+/+  = 2.87 ± 0.21), sleep time was reduced in kcnh4a-/- larvae compared with kcnh4a+/- and kcnh4a+/+  larvae during the night (average: kcnh4a-/- = 13.08 ± 0.27; kcnh4a+/- = 14.78 ± 0.17; and kcnh4a+/+  = 15.46 ± 0.25, t = -6.55, df = 180, p<0.0001, Figure 7B, B').
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 7B, B'.

claim: Sleep time was reduced in kcnh4a-/- larvae compared with kcnh4a+/- and kcnh4a+/+ larvae during the night.
source: Remarkably, while the amount of sleep was similar in all genotypes during the day (average: kcnh4a-/- = 2.76 ± 0.22; kcnh4a+/- = 2.80 ± 0.14; and kcnh4a+/+  = 2.87 ± 0.21), sleep time was reduced in kcnh4a-/- larvae compared with kcnh4a+/- and kcnh4a+/+  larvae during the night (average: kcnh4a-/- = 13.08 ± 0.27; kcnh4a+/- = 14.78 ± 0.17; and kcnh4a+/+  = 15.46 ± 0.25, t = -6.55, df = 180, p<0.0001, Figure 7B, B').
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 7B, B'.

claim: The number of sleep/wake transitions did not change during the day in kcnh4a-/- compared to kcnh4a+/+ larvae.
source: While the number of sleep\wake transitions did not change during the day (kcnh4a-/- = 3.52 ± 0.16; kcnh4a+/+  = 3.79 ± 0.15), their number was decreased in kcnh4a-/- larvae during the night (average: kcnh4a-/- = 12.68 ± 0.19; kcnh4a+/+  = 13.62 ± 0.18, transitions/hr, F[1,80] = 13.16; p<0.0005; df = 80, p<0.0005, Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The number of sleep/wake transitions was decreased in kcnh4a-/- larvae during the night.
source: While the number of sleep\wake transitions did not change during the day (kcnh4a-/- = 3.52 ± 0.16; kcnh4a+/+  = 3.79 ± 0.15), their number was decreased in kcnh4a-/- larvae during the night (average: kcnh4a-/- = 12.68 ± 0.19; kcnh4a+/+  = 13.62 ± 0.18, transitions/hr, F[1,80] = 13.16; p<0.0005; df = 80, p<0.0005, Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The kcnh4a-/- larvae exhibit shorter sleep-bout length specifically during the night.
source: In addition, the kcnh4a-/- larvae exhibit shorter sleep-bout length specifically during the night (average: kcnh4a-/- = 2.21 ± 0.05; kcnh4a+/+  = 2.43 ± 0.05; minhour df = 81, p <0.005, Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The reduction in the number and length of sleep episodes causes global reduction in sleep time during the night in kcnh4a-/- larvae.
source: Thus, the reduction in the number and length of sleep episodes causes global reduction in sleep time during the night in kcnh4a-/- larvae.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined analysis of sleep parameters.

claim: The loss of Kcnh4a affects sleep time and sleep consolidation, specifically during the night.
source: These results show that the loss of Kcnh4a affects sleep time and sleep consolidation, specifically during the night.
evidence: This is inferred from the behavioral data on sleep parameters.

claim: Kcnh4a regulates sleep by repolarization of the membrane potential in sleep-regulating neurons.
source: It also suggests that Kcnh4a regulates sleep by repolarization of the membrane potential in sleep-regulating neurons.
evidence: This is speculated based on the known function of potassium channels and the observed sleep phenotype.

claim: Loss of kcnh4a may reduce potassium efflux and induce repetitive hyperpolarization, and, ultimately, nighttime wakefulness.
source: Since potassiumvoltage-gated channels repolarize the cell membrane (Choe, 2002; Bezanilla, 2000; Swartz, 2008), loss of kcnh4a may reduce potassium efflux and induce repetitive hyperpolarization, and, ultimately, nighttime wakefulness.
evidence: This is speculated based on the known function of potassium channels.

claim: The ether-a-go-go-gene–related (ERG) potassium channel blockers selectively increased waking activity at night in zebrafish.
source: Supporting this role, the ether-a-go-go-gene–related (ERG) potassium channel blockers selectively increased waking activity at night in zebrafish (Rihel et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Rihel et al., 2010.

claim: The shaker gene encodes a voltage-dependent potassium channel and regulates sleep need and efficiency in flies.
source: Genetic screen of fly mutants revealed the short sleeper shaker mutant. The shaker gene encodes a voltage-dependent potassium channel and regulates sleep need and efficiency (Cirelli et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Cirelli et al., 2005.

claim: Loss of the voltage-dependent potassium channel Kcna2 decreases non-rapid-eye-movement (NREM) sleep and increases wakefulness in mice.
source: In mice, loss of the voltage-dependent potassium channel Kcna2 decreases non-rapid-eye-movement (NREM) sleep and increases wakefulness (Douglas et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Douglas et al., 2007.

claim: Sleep is regulated by neuronal-circuit–specific potassium channels in flies, zebrafish, and mammals.
source: These findings suggest that sleep is regulated by neuronal-circuit–specific potassium channels in flies, zebrafish, and mammals.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparative analysis of potassium channel mutants across species.

claim: The presence of Kcnh4a in the excitatory Hcrt neurons suggests that Kcnh4a regulates their activity and, ultimately, sleep and wake.
source: According to this model, in zebrafish, the presence of Kcnh4a in the excitatory Hcrt neurons suggests that Kcnh4a regulates their activity and, ultimately, sleep and wake.
evidence: This is speculated based on the expression pattern and function of Kcnh4a.

claim: In kcnh4a-/- larvae, the absence of Kcnh4a may cause hyperexcitability of the Hcrt neurons that induces the activity of downstream arousal-promoting targets.
source: In kcnh4a-/- larvae, the absence of Kcnh4a may cause hyperexcitability of the Hcrt neurons that induces the activity of downstream arousal-promoting targets, such as the paraventricular thalamic nucleus (Huang et al., 2006) and the locus coeruleus (Carter et al., 2010).
evidence: This is speculated based on the known function of Hcrt neurons and supported by citations.

claim: Eight genes (rfx4, lhx9, scg2, vgll2, ptprn, creb3l1, sgsm1, and fam46a) are found in both zebrafish and mice Hcrt-neuron–specific candidate genes.
source: Comparison between the Hcrt-neuron–specific candidate genes isolated in zebrafish and mice (Dalal et al., 2013) showed that eight genes (rfx4, lhx9, scg2, vgll2, ptprn, creb3l1, sgsm1, and fam46a) are found in both vertebrates.
evidence: This is based on comparison with data from Dalal et al., 2013.

claim: The neuropeptide VF precursor (npvf) and its receptor (npffr1) regulate nociception, anxiety, learning, and memory.
source: The neuropeptide VF precursor (npvf) and its receptor (npffr1) regulate nociception, anxiety, learning, and memory (Liu et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2001.

claim: The NPVF/NPFFR1 system controls pain and analgesia through interactions with the opioid system.
source: The NPVF/NPFFR1 system also controls pain and analgesia through interactions with the opioid system (Liu et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2001.

claim: The nociceptin/orphanin FQ (N/OFQ) system makes synaptic contacts with Hcrt neurons, inhibiting their activity via pre- and post-synaptic mechanisms.
source: This system makes synaptic contacts with Hcrt neurons, inhibiting their activity via pre- and post-synaptic mechanisms.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the N/OFQ system.

claim: Hcrt neurons are essential in the generation of stress-induced analgesia (SIA).
source: More specifically, Hcrt neurons are essential in the generation of stress-induced analgesia (SIA), and N/OFQ blocks SIA via inhibition of Hcrt neuron activity (Xie et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Xie et al., 2008.

claim: N/OFQ blocks SIA via inhibition of Hcrt neuron activity.
source: More specifically, Hcrt neurons are essential in the generation of stress-induced analgesia (SIA), and N/OFQ blocks SIA via inhibition of Hcrt neuron activity (Xie et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Xie et al., 2008.

claim: NPVF/NPFFR and Hcrt neurons may interact in the hypothalamus to regulate morphine- and stress-induced analgesia.
source: Altogether, NPVF/NPFFR and Hcrt neurons may interact in the hypothalamus to regulate morphine- and stress-induced analgesia.
evidence: This is speculated based on the known functions of these systems.
